reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: Typically presents in young adults, more often men, with insidious chronic low back pain and stiffness that improves with activity and worsens with rest, especially in the second half of the night
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes and buttock pain from sacroiliitis are characteristic inflammatory back pain features
Progressive loss of spinal mobility can be assessed with the modified Schober test and chest expansion measurement
Enthesitis (notably at the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia) and asymmetric large-joint peripheral arthritis are common
Extra-articular manifestations include acute anterior uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis
Strongly associated with HLA-B27, though a positive test alone is neither diagnostic nor required
Early sacroiliitis is often better seen on MRI (bone marrow oedema) before radiographic changes such as sclerosis, erosions, and eventual ankylosis appear
Management combines a regular exercise and physiotherapy programme with NSAIDs first-line, escalating to biologic therapy (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors) for inadequate control
reference.pathophysiology: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton and the prototype of the seronegative spondyloarthritides. Inflammation centres on the entheses (sites where ligaments and tendons attach to bone) and the sacroiliac joints. A strong genetic association with HLA-B27 implicates aberrant antigen presentation and dysregulated IL-23/IL-17 pathway signalling. Chronic enthesitis and osteitis drive a cycle of erosion followed by reactive new bone formation, leading to syndesmophyte development, bony bridging across vertebrae, and ultimately spinal fusion (the 'bamboo spine').
additionalDifferentials: Mechanical or degenerative low back pain
Arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the sacroiliac joints to detect early active inflammation before radiographic change
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and spine for sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes, and ankylosis
HLA-B27 typing to support the diagnosis in the right clinical context
Inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR), which may be normal despite active disease
Assessment of extra-articular features including ophthalmology review for uveitis
redFlags: Acute painful red eye suggesting anterior uveitis requiring urgent ophthalmology assessment
New or worsening neurological deficit, or acute severe pain after minor trauma, raising concern for spinal fracture through a rigid fused spine
Symptoms of cardiac conduction block or aortic regurgitation from cardiac involvement
Restrictive lung disease or apical pulmonary fibrosis
reference.prognosis: Disease course is variable; many patients maintain good function with exercise and modern therapy, but persistent inflammation can lead to progressive spinal ankylosis, fixed kyphotic deformity, and increased fracture risk. Early diagnosis and biologic therapy have improved symptom control and quality of life.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic back pain in a young adult to mechanical causes and delaying diagnosis for years
Relying on HLA-B27 as a diagnostic test rather than a supportive finding
Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active disease
Overlooking the high fracture risk of a rigid, osteoporotic spine after minor trauma
Neglecting extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, bowel disease, and cardiac involvement
